newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Diverse deals with APP, EIB.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Diverse deals with APP, EIB.

text.p: Asian debt markets offered a diverse group of deals on Tuesday.
APP Global Finance launched a secured US$500 million five-year floating rate note issue via lead manager UBS Singapore. The transaction has a complex structure.

Proceeds of the issue ultimately will be used by Asia Pulp and Paper (APP), the New York-listed, Singapore-headquartered Indonesian pulp and paper producer. But APP has no ownership control, either directly or indirectly, in the borrower.
Rather, APP Global Finance is a special purpose vehicle of APP Global Ltd, the controlling shareholder of APP.
Global currently holds 86.2 percent of the issued ordinary shares of APP but it is not a member of the APP Group.
The primary purpose of the issuer is to issue the notes and to invest in and hold redeemable preference shares issued by Finance (I), a wholly owned subsidiary of APP.
Finance (1) will use proceeds of the share sale to subscribe from APP an FRN due 2001 (called the APP note) in a principal amount equal to the principal amount of the APP Global Finance note.
That's how Asia Pulp and Paper ultimately gets the funds.
The APP Global Finance notes will be secured by a pledge by Global of 50.1 percent of the outstanding voting stock of APP and a pledge by Finance (1).

APP Global Finance expects the interest and principal payments on the APP note to serve as a source of funding for Finance (1) to make dividend and redemption payments under the redeemable preference shares, which in turn will be a source of funding for the issuer to make payments on the notes.
Asian bankers have expressed reservations about the deal because of the pledge of shares as security. They said they would rather see fixed assets put up as security.
More information on the transaction, and on bankers' reaction to its structure, is expected to emerge this week as the deal currently is roadshowing in Asia.
Among other deals of the day, the European Investment Bank launched a HK$1 billion five-year fixed rate bond.

The AAA-rated bond pays a semi-annual coupon of 7.62 percent and was priced to yield 33.6 basis points over comparable Hong Kong Monetary Authority Exchange Fund Notes or 90.8 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.

Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said the issue should do well because HK$ fixed-rate issuance, with the exception of government issues, had hit a dry spell after a deluge of deals a few months ago.
"The market has had two months to absorb the flood of new issues so the timing is all right," he said.
Application will be made to the HKMA to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
Institutional investors, which are more likely to take on the fixed-rate paper, get no such benefit from LAF.
But Fung said there is a perception that LAF issues are more liquid -- if only because they tend to be larger than non-LAF issues -- and that entices institutional investors.
In London, KEXIM's US$500 million five-year bond was priced to yield 44 basis points over Treasuries, on the wide side of the indicated range. Nomura International and SBC Warburg were leads.
Korea Long-Term Credit Bank is seen launching a Euro-Australian dollar bond soon.
And Tingyi Noodles' US$150 million FRN is due Wednesday. ING Barings is the lead for the issue, which is seen paying 125 basis points all-in for five years.
